strengths: The paper addresses an important explanatory question: why learning return distributions can improve reinforcement learning. Connecting distributional objectives to regularization and optimization is a potentially useful research direction.

The comparison of SAC and distributional SAC, each with and without policy entropy, across eight continuous-control tasks and five seeds provides useful empirical observations about their interaction.

For fixed features and a linear softmax head, the histogram cross-entropy loss does have bounded gradients, convexity, and smoothness. The appendices and hyperparameter table make the proposed analysis and experimental setup easier to inspect.
weaknesses: The foundational expectation decomposition in Eq. 4 does not hold for general return distributions. Writing P = (1−epsilon) delta_mean + epsilon mu with a probability distribution mu requires P to have mass at least 1−epsilon exactly at its mean. For example, Uniform[−1,1] has no atom at zero, so the proposed residual assigns negative mass there for every 0 < epsilon < 1. Although the text introduces a restricted mixture family, it subsequently claims general attainability without showing that Bellman updates preserve this family. The atomic component also conflicts with the continuous-density treatment of KL. Consequently, the central regularization interpretation is not established for the algorithms studied.

The policy-improvement argument in Section 3.3 and Appendix D is mathematically ill-defined. Its KL objective uses the scalar cross-entropy H(mu,q) as its first argument, although KL requires probability distributions. The subsequent policy-improvement inequality therefore does not follow. More fundamentally, decomposing a critic-fitting objective does not establish equivalence to adding a cross-entropy penalty to rewards, as Eq. 7 does. The claim that this penalty encourages visiting dispersed return distributions is also unsupported; when q matches mu, minimizing cross-entropy favors lower entropy.

The acceleration theorem does not establish the advertised comparison. Its 'expectation-based RL' baseline minimizes cross-entropy against a point mass at the mean, rather than the squared-error objective introduced in Eq. 2. Theorem 3 specifies epsilon = 1/(1+tau), whereas Appendix I uses epsilon = 1/(1+kappa); with the stated choice, the variance bound generally retains an O(tau) term and does not yield the claimed tau-squared stationarity guarantee. The baseline proof also changes the stated fixed learning rate to one that decreases with the target accuracy. These are substantive inconsistencies in a central result.

The stability comparison overstates what is proved. Theorem 2 concerns SGD on a fixed dataset with fixed features and a convex softmax head; it does not establish stability of learned neural representations, changing Bellman targets, or the Adam-trained actor-critic systems evaluated. The assertion that squared loss lacks smoothness is incorrect under the same linear-feature setting: its Hessian is bounded when features are bounded. Globally bounded gradients are a distinct property. The remaining valid observation largely specializes established histogram-loss and SGD-stability results, limiting its independent contribution.

Proposition 1(2) lacks necessary assumptions. KL convergence implies total-variation convergence, but does not generally imply Wasserstein convergence on an unbounded return space without additional moment or tail control. Appendix B invokes a compact-space argument without establishing the corresponding conditions.

The experiments do not isolate or validate the proposed mechanisms. They use IQN-style quantile regression with a Huber loss, whereas the theory analyzes histogram KL loss, and they do not implement the newly defined policy-improvement operator. Smaller raw gradient norms can arise from loss scaling, bounded Huber derivatives, or architecture differences and do not demonstrate uniform stability. Neither the residual distribution, the kappa condition, nor increased exploration of dispersed-return states is measured. Return curves therefore cannot verify the specific regularization explanation or acceleration theorem.

Reproducibility and clarity remain incomplete despite the hyperparameter table. Appendix K refers to an existing implementation but does not provide the precise modified implementation or a complete evaluation protocol; the plotted uncertainty bands are not defined, and the modified quantile-sampling formula is incomplete. These omissions limit verification of the empirical comparisons. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the simulated experiments; the rejection is driven by fundamental technical deficiencies.
